title: A car for every Indian family
hook: A failed car company, no car experts, and a huge goal. Can you build India's first family car?

profit.label: Sales
profit.hint: Cars made and money coming in today

future.label: Future
future.hint: How strong Maruti will be in the years ahead

intro.text: Gurgaon, 1981. Ten years ago, a company here promised to make a small car for Indian families, but it made only a handful before it shut down. Now the government is trying again. The new company is called Maruti Udyog, and you are in charge.

s_goal.text: Your goal is to make 1 lakh cars a year, but all of India buys fewer than 40,000 cars a year, mostly big, old Ambassadors and Padminis. Nobody on your team has built a car before, so you need a foreign carmaker to teach your people how.

d1.title: Find a partner
d1.setup: Fiat, Volkswagen, Renault, Peugeot and Nissan have all said no, and most other carmakers want their own people to run your factory. Daihatsu of Japan looked like your best hope for months, but now it plans to build with another Indian company. A few days later, Suzuki, a smaller Japanese carmaker, sends a message. It wants in.
d1.question: Who do you build India's car with?
d1.advisor: We cannot afford another failed start, so we need to move quickly. But the company we choose will shape how Maruti works for years.

options.label: Keep talking to Daihatsu, but risk losing more time
options.outcome: You spend months trying to bring Daihatsu back. Late in the year it agrees to help, but India is not its main concern, so it sends only a small team. You are already late before the first machine arrives.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Maruti needed to learn how to build cars, so it needed a partner keen to teach. Daihatsu was not keen, so it sent little help, and you spent months waiting for it.
options.better: Go with the partner that comes to you hungry, even if it is smaller and less famous.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you waited on a partner that had stopped caring.

options.label: Talk to Suzuki, but risk a smaller, unknown maker
options.outcome: Talks begin in April 1982. Suzuki's president meets your team himself, and Suzuki offers more money than any other company. On 2 October 1982 you sign the deal. Suzuki buys about a quarter of Maruti and plans to own more later.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Maruti needed to learn how to build cars in India. Suzuki was ready to teach, and your people went to Japan to learn, so Maruti's own team gained the skills.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you picked the hungry partner over the famous one.

options.label: Let a foreign maker run the plant, but lose control
options.outcome: A foreign carmaker signs quickly. Its managers and machines arrive, and work begins fast. But your Indian staff mostly stand and watch, while the foreign managers make every big decision far away.
options.why: Remember: own your core skill, and get help with the rest. Maruti had to learn how to build cars. If the foreign company did everything, your team would not learn, and you would have a factory that others must run.
options.better: Pick a partner that will train your own people and help Indian suppliers grow.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you bought a factory instead of learning to build one.

d2.title: Which car first?

setup.text: Suzuki has three vehicles you could make: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly in cities. But one board member wants Maruti to make work vehicles, not cars.

Daihatsu has three vehicles you could make: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly in cities. But one board member wants Maruti to make work vehicles, not cars.

Your partner has three vehicles you could make: a tiny four-seat car, a small van and a light jeep. A survey shows that 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly in cities. But one board member wants Maruti to make work vehicles, not cars.

d2.question: What do you build first?
d2.advisor: More models could bring in different buyers. But each model needs its own parts, tools and training, and we have never built even one.

options.label: Build the small car first, but offer less space

outcome.text: You choose a car based on Suzuki's 1979 Alto. It has a small 796 cc engine, and you name it the Maruti 800. Its front-wheel drive and disc brakes will be new to Indian buyers.
Your partner's small car is light and cheap to run, which is just what city families need, although it will take work to make it ready for Indian roads.

options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs. One car meant one set of parts, one line and one kind of training. It was also a car most families could afford, and the van and jeep could come later.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you built one car, the one most families could use and afford.

options.label: Build all three models, but take on more work
options.outcome: You make all three vehicles at once. Your new factory needs three sets of parts, three sets of tools and three kinds of training, and your workers must learn much more. Every line moves slowly, and the December launch date starts to slip.
options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs. Three vehicles meant three times the parts to find and the skills to learn, in a plant that had never built even one.
options.better: Build one vehicle well first, the small car, and add the others once the plant runs smoothly.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you tried to build three vehicles before you could build one.

options.label: Build the van first, but charge families more
options.outcome: Shopkeepers and taxi owners like the idea, because a van can carry a big family or goods. But it costs more than the small car, and families who ride scooters still cannot afford a car, which is why Maruti was started.
options.why: Remember: every extra model adds hidden costs. You kept things simple by choosing one model, but that model mainly helped shops and taxis. Maruti was meant to give Indian families a car they could afford.
options.better: Build the small car first, and add the van soon after.
options.takeaway: In 1982 you started with a useful van, but missed the biggest need.

text.text: The launch is set for December 1983, but your plant is learning three vehicles at once. You still need hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and dealers across the country.

The launch date is December 1983. You have just 14 months to build a factory, find hundreds of Indian companies to make parts, and choose dealers across the country. Your people fly to Japan to learn how Suzuki builds cars.
The launch is set for December 1983, and Daihatsu's slow start has eaten into your time. You still need a factory, hundreds of Indian firms to make parts, and dealers across the country.
The launch is set for December 1983. Your partner's managers are building the factory fast, and they want to bring almost every part from abroad. You still need dealers across the country.

d3.title: Make the date
d3.setup: The factory is taking shape, but there's a problem. Indian parts makers are not ready: some parts are good, others are not, and deliveries often come late. If you wait for them to improve, you will miss the December launch.
d3.question: How do you make the launch date?
d3.advisor: We promised a car in December, and waiting puts that date at risk. But buying parts from abroad means less of our first car is made in India.

options.label: Wait for better Indian parts, but launch a year late
options.outcome: You wait for Indian suppliers to improve. December comes and goes without a car. Newspapers begin calling Maruti another failed dream, and Delhi starts asking why the project is late.
options.why: Remember: find the longest chain of work, and buy ready-made anything that could make you late. Indian parts were that chain, so waiting for them made the whole launch wait.
options.better: Launch on time with imported parts, and set firm dates for switching to Indian ones.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you put a perfect car ahead of an on-time car.

options.label: Use Indian parts now, but risk quality problems
options.outcome: You launch on time with the Indian parts you have, but their quality is uneven. Within weeks, buyers return to dealers with leaks, rattles and breakdowns, and they say the new Maruti is no better than the old cars.
options.why: Remember: buy ready-made anything that could make you late, then learn to make it. You kept the date with parts that were not ready, and a car built from them broke down in front of everyone.
options.better: Use proven imported parts at first, and raise Indian suppliers to the new standard step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you chose a local label over real quality.

options.label: Use Japanese parts now, but depend on imports first

outcome.text: Your workers put together kits shipped from Japan. The first 192 cars are ready in December 1983, and only the tyres and batteries are Indian, less than 3% of the car. You promise to reach 95% Indian parts within five years.
You put together parts shipped from abroad. Very little of the vehicle is Indian yet, but you now have a firm plan to change that.

options.why: Remember: find the longest chain of work, and buy ready-made anything that could make you late. Indian parts were delaying the cars, so kits from Japan let you launch on time, and a five-year plan meant you would still make the parts yourself.
options.takeaway: In 1983 you launched on time and made a firm plan to go local.

text.text: 14 December 1983, New Delhi. The Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi, hands the keys of the first Maruti 800 to its owner, an Indian Airlines employee who paid ₹47,500. The plant, the suppliers and the dealers were all built in 14 months.
Your first vehicles rolled out on time in December 1983, but the repair bills are growing, and so are the jokes about Maruti.
December 1983. Your first vehicle rolls out of Gurgaon on time, with the press watching. Now you will find out how many people want one.
Late 1984. Almost a year behind plan, your first vehicle finally rolls out of Gurgaon, and this one is mostly Indian. People are glad to see it, but many had stopped believing it would ever come.
1984. Months behind plan, your first vehicles finally roll out of Gurgaon. Learning three vehicles at once slowed every line, and the papers have started to joke about Maruti.

d4.title: How will the plant work?

setup.text: About 1,20,000 people have booked a Maruti, but your factory can make only about 20,000 this year. More machines need foreign money, and India has very little to spare. So you walk through the factory, looking for ways to make more cars with what you already have.

Far more people have booked than you can supply. Delhi now wants your own managers to run the shop floor, not your partner's. More machines need foreign money that India lacks, so every extra car must come from this plant.
Far more people have booked than you can supply this year. More machines need foreign money, and India has very little to spare. So every extra car must come from the plant you already have.

d4.question: How will you run the plant?
d4.advisor: Our shop heads know their workers and like running things their own way. The partner's way is one strict set of rules for everyone, managers too. We must decide how much to change.

options.label: Let shop heads choose their methods, but accept different results
options.outcome: Each shop follows its own method. The weld shop and the paint shop check cars differently, so a car passes one check but fails the next. Workers argue about which method is right, and the number of cars made each day grows slowly.
options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and mistakes. With every shop following its own method, mistakes were harder to find, and you couldn't tell which method worked best or teach it to everyone.
options.better: Pick one way for every job, write it down, and train everyone in it, bosses included.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you let every shop work its own way.

options.label: Use your partner's rules in every shop, but end manager perks

outcome.text: Officers and workers eat the same food in one canteen and work in open offices. Shifts begin with exercises, tea breaks are short, and floors stay clean. Everyone keeps training, and in 1984–85 Gurgaon makes more than its target of 20,000 cars.

Bosses and workers follow the same rules, from the first exercise of the shift to the last check on the line. Every worker is trained in the same way, and month by month more cars roll out right first time.

options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and mistakes. When everyone followed the same steps, mistakes were easy to find, and when one team found a better way, every team could learn it.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you ran the whole plant one standard way, bosses included.

options.label: Add another shift now, but train new workers as they work
options.outcome: You bring in new workers and start another shift, and more cars leave each day. But the new workers copy whoever stands beside them, so each learns a different method. Small faults appear, and more buyers return to dealers for repairs.
options.why: Remember: one standard way of working cuts cost and mistakes. More hands helped, but with no single way to learn, every new worker learned a slightly different job.
options.better: Set one standard way first, train everyone in it, then add the shift.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you added hands before you had one way of working.

d5.title: Build Indian suppliers

setup.text: Parts keep arriving from abroad: less than a tenth of each car is made in India so far, and every imported part uses foreign money. You promised to change that. For each part, you need Indian firms that can make it well, and most can't yet.
Your Indian parts break too often, and buyers are angry. Hundreds of Indian firms must learn to make much better parts, or your vehicles will never be trusted.
Your partner's managers want to keep buying from their own suppliers abroad, and every imported part costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms are waiting for a chance.
Your Indian suppliers are making parts now, but their quality is uneven, and hundreds of them must learn to work to a higher standard.
Too many parts still come from abroad, and every one costs foreign money. Hundreds of Indian firms must learn to work to a higher standard.

d5.question: How do you choose your suppliers?
d5.advisor: Choosing a few firms means bigger orders for them, but many others get no work. Choosing many spreads the orders, but each firm gets less work to learn from.

options.label: Pick a few firms for each part on quality, but leave most out

outcome.text: A powerful politician asks to supply parts. Your team tells him to bring a sample for testing, like everyone else, and he never returns. Hundreds of firms must change their machines and their ways of working, and once they see Maruti will succeed, they take it seriously.
You hold every supplier to one standard, and you test them all, even the well-connected ones. It is slow and painful, but parts start arriving on time and fitting right.

options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them. Large orders gave these firms a reason to buy better machines and improve, which made Maruti's cars cheaper, better and more Indian.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you chose a few strong suppliers on merit and pushed them hard.

options.label: Give many firms orders for each part, but each gets less work
options.outcome: Politicians across the states are pleased, and hundreds of small firms begin making parts. But each gets only a small order, so it has little chance to improve. Parts still differ in quality, and making cars stays costly.
options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them. With orders spread thin, no firm made enough parts to pay for better machines or to learn properly.
options.better: Pick a few strong firms on quality alone, give them big orders and train them hard.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you spread your orders thin and nobody got good.

options.label: Buy more parts abroad, but spend India's scarce foreign money
options.outcome: You keep buying most parts from abroad. The cars stay good and the factory keeps running, but every car uses foreign money, and Delhi grows unhappy. Indian parts makers get few orders, so they have little chance to learn.
options.why: Remember: pick a few strong suppliers on quality, and push them to get better. Buying abroad kept quality safe, but it built no Indian supplier, used up foreign money and broke your promise to go local.
options.better: Choose Indian suppliers on quality alone and help them improve, so the car becomes Indian step by step.
options.takeaway: In 1984 you played safe with imports and built no local strength.

text.text: It is 1987, and Maruti is growing fast. A van joined the 800 in 1984, and the Gypsy jeep followed in 1985. In 1986 the 1,00,000th Maruti rolled out, and the 800 got a newer body. Yet Indian buyers still wait years for a car.
It is 1987. Your parts now come from all over India, but quality is uneven, and many small firms can't keep up with your orders.
It is 1987. Your cars sell, but each shop still works its own way, and faults that one shop fixes keep coming back in another.
It is 1987. The extra shift made more cars, and you are slowly teaching everyone one way of working, but the repair bills from those early months still hurt.
It is 1987. Your vehicles are on Indian roads, and people are still queuing for them. Now you have to decide how far to push Maruti.

d6.title: Sell abroad?

setup.text: Indian families still wait years for their Marutis, so you could sell every car you make at home. But you are thinking about selling in Europe too. Suzuki and the head of your board both warn you not to try.

Indian families still wait years for their cars, so you could sell everything you make at home. But you are thinking about selling in Europe too. Your partner and the head of your board both warn you not to try.

d6.question: What do you do next?
d6.advisor: Selling in Europe could bring in foreign money. But buyers there expect more, and a failure abroad would hurt Maruti's name at home.

options.label: Sell only in India, but miss the chance to earn foreign money
options.outcome: You keep every car for Indian buyers, sales stay strong, and your partner and board are pleased. But with no demanding buyers abroad, quality improves slowly, and when other carmakers enter India years later, Maruti is less ready than it should be.
options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out. With a long queue at home, nobody pushed you to improve.
options.better: Sell some cars abroad to learn from tougher buyers, even while the queue at home is long.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you stayed home and missed a chance to raise your game.

options.label: Send a third to Europe, but make Indian buyers wait longer
options.outcome: Thousands of Marutis leave for Europe, and families at home must wait years longer. Many exported cars need changes to meet Europe's rules, so they sit at the port while your engineers work on them. Families ask why buyers abroad get Marutis first.
options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out, but start small so you can learn. A small batch would have taught you the same lessons without making every Indian buyer wait longer.
options.better: Send a small first batch abroad to learn, and grow exports as your plant gets better.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you bet a third of your cars on buyers you had never met.

options.label: Send a small first batch to Europe, but risk a poor response

outcome.text: You send 500 cars to Hungary, and the first arrive on 24 October 1987. France follows in 1989, and the Netherlands in 1990. To meet Europe's rules, you add seat belts to the Maruti 800, which never had them before.
Selling abroad pushes your plant and your suppliers toward world standards, and buyers in other countries start to notice your vehicles.

options.why: Remember: tough buyers make you better, so seek them out. Europe's buyers and rules pushed you to raise your standards, and a small first batch kept the risk small.
options.takeaway: In 1987 you went abroad to get better, not just bigger.

text.text: By 1988, your Gurgaon factory can make 1,00,000 cars a year: the goal set in 1981. The Maruti 800 stays on sale until 2014, and nearly 29 lakh are built. In 2024, about 4 in every 10 cars sold in India are still Marutis.
You built the people's car, one standard way of working and a strong group of Indian suppliers around it. For millions of families, a Maruti becomes their first car.

survivor.title: A good company, a smaller dream

text.text: Maruti builds three good vehicles, but they arrive too late or cost too much for many families. It never becomes India's family car, and when foreign carmakers enter India in the 1990s, they win the buyers Maruti had hoped to reach.
Maruti's vans are everywhere, carrying goods and families. But the small family car comes late, and when foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, Maruti is a strong player, not the clear leader.
Maruti makes good cars and good money, but it never becomes the car of every Indian family. When foreign rivals arrive in the 1990s, it is a strong player, not the clear leader.

collapse.title: Another failed dream
collapse.text: Your cars cost too much or break down too often, and Indian parts makers never get the chance to improve. Like the first Maruti, your company becomes known for a big promise to Indian families that it failed to keep.

fired.title: Delhi lets you go
fired.text: Delhi has seen enough. After three costly decisions, the government, which owns Maruti, removes you from your job, and Indian families must wait for a new boss to try again.

realHistory: In 1981 the government started Maruti Udyog, a company with no car experience. In October 1982 it signed with Suzuki, a late but eager partner, and in just 14 months it built a factory in Gurgaon, a group of suppliers and a dealer network. The first Maruti 800 was handed over on 14 December 1983. About 1,20,000 people booked in the first year, far more than Maruti could make. It ran its plant the Japanese way, with one canteen and open offices for officers and workers alike. Maruti pushed hundreds of Indian suppliers to raise their quality, began exporting to Europe in 1987, and could make 1,00,000 cars a year by 1988. The 800 stayed on sale until 2014, and Maruti Suzuki is still India's biggest carmaker.
